newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia woos oil investors with sweet talk.
newsitem.headline: Colombia woos oil investors with sweet talk.

text.p: Venezuela may be ahead in Latin America's race for foreign investors in the oil sector, but Colombia is trying to catch some of its wind and has some advantages over its neighbour, Colombian officials said at a conference this week.

In the first bilateral conference between U.S. firms and Colombia since decertification earlier this year, Colombia wooed multinationals with promises of sweeter terms in oil exploration contracts and heftier security measures.

Colombian Energy and Mines Minister Rodrigo Villamizar said 80 percent of the country's oil-bearing rocks had yet to be explored and the country faced a sharp drop in oil exports by 2000 unless more work was done now.

Colombia is living an oil boom at the moment, with production forecasted to rise another 350,000 to one million barrels per day (bpd) just after 2000. But Villamizar saw it tailing off sharply after that, hitting 400,000 bpd in 2006 when Colombia would become an oil importer if no new reserves were found.
"Colombia has petroleum reserves but it is not exploiting them fully... so Colombia has to develop policies that attract foreign investors," said U.S. ambassador to Colombia Myles Frechette.
Delegates said that high tax rates and security risks were two major obstacles to investment.
The problems of sabotage were highlighted by Occidental boss Stephen Newton who said the Cano Limon oil pipeline was being blown up by guerrillas at a rate of 45-50 times a year.
One delegate at the conference said security measures could add as much as 10-15 percent to operating costs in Colombia.

"Here in Colombia we may have security problems, but we also have a long history of macroeconomic stability, we follow the rules of the game, the country is growing, we don't change our minds all the time and inflation is under control," Colombian President Ernesto Samper told journalists.
He said that of 19,000 voluntary soldiers in the Colombian Army, 11,000 were used to protect energy installations.

Minister Villamizar proposed setting up a new security fund, paid for by oil operators, which would administer security arrangements centrally. Companies were unhappy negotiating individual protection directly with the Colombian army.
The minister also said that he was considering more lenient terms for high-risk oil exploration contracts, after Colombia drilled just 30 wells last year, against over 1000 in Venezuela.

Using a formula similar to that used in Venezuela's successful "marginal fields" initiative, Colombia has already drawn up new contracts to encourage greater output from existing oilfields and attract investment in small fields.
But investors said this was not enough to make Colombia competitive in the world oil exploration market.
Colombia's total tax take in oil projects was one of the highest in the world at 83 percent, which did not reflect the high costs of operating there, industry delegates said.

"We are entering a new phase -- a discussion phase for the moment -- to take decisions that will change the terms of the contracts to encourage more exploration work, not just in oil but hydrocarbons in general," Villamizar said.

Antonio Urdinola, an economist who now heads Colombia's state oil company Ecopetrol, said: "We have to make large changes to some contracts... In some areas we have scarce information and high risks. We see that these areas are not being exploited and we must attract private national and foreign capital."
Colombia hopes to attract $18 billion investment in the upstream oil sector by the year 2000.
Urdinola proposed a system of exploration contracts for private investors where the market would determine the participation rates of Ecopetrol through an open bidding round.
"We hope to do it in the near future," he said. "The market would set the conditions and the risks."
